title: Best Ways to Redeem Bilt Rewards Points
summary: Bilt points are worth about 0.55¢ as statement credit but 2–5¢ transferred to World of Hyatt, Alaska, and other partners. Every redemption ranked, all 16 transfer partners, and the sweet spots worth booking.
body_text: The quick answer What to actually do with your Bilt points Bilt points transfer 1:1 to a short but unusually good roster — World of Hyatt plus a set of airlines you can't reach from most other cards. That's the whole game. Redeem for statement credit or rent and a point is worth around half a cent. Move it to Hyatt or Alaska and it's worth 2¢, 4¢, sometimes more. The floor is low and the ceiling is high, so the exit is everything. The four rules that matter Transfer to travel partners. Never take statement credit, rent, or the Bilt Collection. World of Hyatt is the crown jewel: 1:1, with award nights from 3,500 points. On airlines, lead with the rare ones: Alaska, American, Flying Blue, Turkish, Aeroplan. Skip the Bilt Collection, Amazon, Lyft, rent, and Hilton/Marriott transfers — all well under 1¢. Roame fair value 2.05¢ per point A realistic average when you transfer to Hyatt or airline partners. Point value What your Bilt points are actually worth A point has no fixed value — it depends entirely on the exit. Bilt's built-in options set a brutal floor: the Bilt Collection merchandise store can price a paper-towel roll at 3,000 points, and statement credit hovers near 0.55¢. Transfers are the whole reason to hold the currency. Here's the spread you're choosing between every time you redeem. 0.3¢ Bilt Collection The true floor. In what world does a paper towel cost 3,000 points? 0.55¢ Statement credit & rent Rent runs ~0.7¢ (1.05¢ on Rent Day). Convenient, never worth it. 2–5¢ Hyatt & airline transfers Where the whole program pays off. Bilt has no travel portal that boosts point value — there is no 1.25¢ or 1.5¢ "book travel" tier the way Chase and Amex offer. The only route above 1¢ is transferring to a partner, which makes partner choice the single most important decision you make. Ranked Every redemption, best to worst The same points, ranked by what they're worth. Start at the top and only move down when availability forces you to. 1 World of Hyatt award nights Off-peak nights from 3,500 points; top-tier resorts that would cost $1,000+ cash. 2–5¢ 2 Alaska Mileage Plan partner awards Bilt is the only non-airline transfer partner. JAL, Cathay, and Qantas premium cabins. 2–4¢ 3 International business & first class Turkish, Flying Blue, Aeroplan, Virgin Atlantic. A $5,000 fare for ~60k points. 2–4¢ 4 American AAdvantage sweet spots A rare transfer route to AA — oneworld awards and web-special pricing. 1.8–3¢ 5 Accor Live Limitless (Rent Day) Fixed-value ~1.5¢ against Sofitel & Fairmont, best stacked with a transfer bonus. ~1.5¢ 6 Rent, statement credit, Amazon, Lyft, Collection You are leaving 65–85% of the value behind. The Bilt Collection is the worst at ~0.3¢. 0.3–0.7¢ Transfer partners Every Bilt transfer partner Points transfer to a compact roster — but a distinctive one. Everything moves at a clean 1:1 , and Bilt is one of the only transferable currencies that reaches Alaska and American . That rarity, not the length of the list, is the edge. Airlines · 11 programs Airline Program Ratio Why it matters Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan 1:1 The headline partner — the only non-airline currency that transfers into Mileage Plan American Airlines AAdvantage 1:1 Rare among transferable points; oneworld premium cabins Air France–KLM Flying Blue 1:1 Europe from 25k economy; monthly Promo Rewards United MileagePlus 1:1 Deep Star Alliance network and dynamic saver space Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1:1 7,500 mi domestic United; cheap Star Alliance business Air Canada Aeroplan 1:1 Star Alliance, sub-500-mi economy from 6k points Virgin Atlantic Flying Club 1:1 ANA & Delta One sweet spots; frequent transfer bonuses Cathay Pacific Cathay 1:1 First & business to Asia with low surcharges Emirates Skywards 1:1 First-class shower spa to Dubai · watch surcharges Avianca LifeMiles 1:1 Star Alliance business with no fuel surcharges Southwest Rapid Rewards 1:1 Domestic economy at a fixed ~1.3–1.5¢; points count toward Companion Pass Hotels · 5 programs Hotel Program Ratio Why it matters Hyatt World of Hyatt 1:1 The crown jewel — award nights from 3,500 points IHG IHG One Rewards 1:1 Fourth-night-free and occasional cheap luxury nights Accor Live Limitless 1:1 Fixed-value ~1.5¢; ideal with a Rent Day bonus Marriott Bonvoy 1:1 Recently devalued — Bonvoy points worth far less. Avoid Hilton Honors 1:1 Honors points ~0.4¢ each — a steep downgrade. Avoid Hyatt is the only hotel transfer worth making by default. Hilton and Marriott convert 1:1 but their points are worth a fraction of a Bilt point — a straight downgrade. Accor is fixed-value (~1.5¢) and only makes sense against a specific stay, ideally stacked with a Rent Day transfer bonus. Sweet spots Four bookings that prove the point Real redemptions where your Bilt points go furthest — overwater villas, lie-flat seats, and Manhattan suites. Every one of these beats paying cash by thousands of dollars. Maldives ~5.4¢/pt World of Hyatt Park Hyatt · overwater villa 35k pts ~$1,900 value Off-peak nights at the Park Hyatt Maldives run 35k points against cash rates north of $1,900. The single most lucrative thing you can do with Bilt. Tokyo ~4.3¢/pt Alaska Mileage Plan JAL business · one way 60k pts ~$5,200 value Alaska prices JAL business to Japan at a flat 60k one-way. Bilt is one of the only ways to feed Mileage Plan without flying Alaska. Paris ~5.3¢/pt Flying Blue Business · one way 55k pts ~$2,900 value Standardized saver pricing to Europe from anywhere, and monthly Promo Rewards can knock 25% off award tickets before you even transfer. New York ~3.0¢/pt World of Hyatt Park Hyatt · category 7 35k pts ~$1,050 value A Manhattan Park Hyatt night for 35k points instead of $1,000+. Points earned paying your rent, going straight back into a stay near home. Avoid these The worst ways to use Bilt points Bilt makes these effortless because they're the least valuable to you. Each hands back most of your points' worth for the sake of convenience. If you're doing any of them, stop. Bilt Collection ~0.3¢ The merchandise store is the single worst option — everyday goods priced at multiples of retail. A paper towel for 3,000 points is not a deal. Statement credit 0.55¢ Wiping card charges hands back nearly half your points' value. There is no upside and no bonus tier. Never. Rent redemption 0.7¢ Using points toward rent lands around 0.7¢ (1.05¢ on Rent Day). Convenient, but a fraction of transfer value. Amazon "pay with points" 0.7¢ The most efficient non-travel exit — which is damning. Pay with the card and keep the points for a transfer instead. Lyft, fitness, student loans ~0.7¢ All the lifestyle redemptions cluster near cash-back value. Fine only if you genuinely will not travel. Hilton & Marriott transfers <1¢ They move 1:1, but the destination points are worth far less than a Bilt point. A voluntary downgrade — skip both. Earn more How to earn Bilt points fast The redemptions above are only as good as the pile of points behind them. The Bilt Card 2.0 lineup is now three cards — Blue, Obsidian, and Palladium — issued by Column N.A. and serviced by Cardless. All three earn on rent and mortgage with no transaction fee ; what differs is your everyday multipliers and perks. up to 1.25× on rent & mortgage — every card, no transaction fee Housing earning is no longer a flat rate. You pick one of two Bilt-exclusive bonus options that decides how you're rewarded: Housing-only rewards Up to 1.25× points on housing automatically, scaling with your everyday spend that cycle: 0.5× at 25% of rent, 0.75× at 50%, 1× at 75%, 1.25× when everyday spend meets or beats your rent. Below 25%, you still earn 250 points. Flexible Bilt Cash 4% back in Bilt Cash on everyday spend, on top of points. Redeem it dollar-for-dollar across Bilt, or spend $30 of Bilt Cash to unlock 1,000 points on a housing payment — up to 1× with no fee. Everyday Bilt Blue $0 no annual fee 1× Everyday purchases 2× Everyday spend on Rent Day (1st) Neighborhood Benefits: extra points at partner restaurants, fitness studios & pharmacies. Category maximizer Bilt Obsidian $95 annual fee 3× Dining or grocery — pick one yearly (grocery to $25k) 2× Travel 1× All other everyday purchases $100 annual Bilt hotel credit (semi-annual). Rent Day: 6× category, 4× travel. Premium Bilt Palladium $495 annual fee 2× Everyday purchases 4× Everyday spend on Rent Day (1st) $200 Bilt Cash + $400 hotel credit annually, plus Priority Pass lounge access. On Rent Day (the 1st of each month) everyday categories double, up to a 1,000-point bonus — 2× on Blue, up to 6× on Obsidian’s category, 4× on Palladium. All three carry a 10% intro APR for 12 billing cycles, no foreign transaction fees, and free credit reporting on rent. Earn rates and fees are published values; confirm current terms before applying. title: Why asset allocation matters for long-term retirement investing
summary: Learn how asset allocation, diversification, and saving habits may support your long-term retirement investing goals.
body_text: Asset allocation is the process of dividing your investment portfolio across major asset classes (stocks, bonds, and cash) to achieve an appropriate balance between growth potential and mitigation of downside risk. Importantly, it also serves as a primary driver of portfolio performance over time. In general, investors with longer time horizons often hold more of their assets in stocks because they have historically offered higher long‑term returns. As retirement gets closer, typically less volatile bonds and cash often begin to play a larger role by helping reduce portfolio swings while still supporting income and growth needs over time. Figure 1 shows T. Rowe Price’s sample retirement portfolios by age. Younger investors start with a significant allocation to stocks, but that percentage gradually shifts toward bonds and money market assets as they near and move through retirement. Although these examples are age-based and do not reflect personal risk tolerance, they provide a useful visual of how asset allocation can change over time. Sample asset allocation by age for retirement (Fig. 1) These allocations are age‑based only and do not take risk tolerance into account. Our asset allocation models are designed to meet the needs of a hypothetical investor with an assumed retirement age of 65 and a withdrawal horizon of 30 years. The model allocations are based on an analysis that seeks to balance long‑term return potential with anticipated short‑term volatility. The model allocations reflect our view of appropriate levels of trade‑off between potential return and short‑term volatility for investors of certain age ranges. The longer the time frame for investing, the higher the allocation is to stocks (and the higher the volatility) versus bonds or cash. Limitations: While the samples have been designed with reasonable assumptions and methods, the samples are hypothetical only and have certain limitations. — The samples do not take into account individual circumstances or preferences, and the sample displayed for your age may not align with your accumulation time frame, withdrawal horizon, or view of the appropriate levels of trade‑off between potential return and short‑term volatility. — Investing consistent with a sample allocation does not protect against losses or guarantee future results. Please be sure to take other assets, income, and investments into consideration in applying asset allocation models to your individual situation. Other T. Rowe Price educational tools or advice services use different assumptions and methods and may yield different outcomes. close Why your time horizon matters when choosing investments Time horizon refers to how long your money will stay invested before you need to use it. This matters because different asset classes behave differently over time. Historically, stocks have delivered the highest returns among major asset classes over longer periods. However, they also have tended to experience the largest short‑term performance swings. Bonds, on the other hand, have generally produced lower returns than stocks with less variable short‑term returns. Cash has offered the most stability, but with the lowest long‑term return potential. Combining these asset classes allows you to manage that trade‑off of growth potential with short‑term volatility. Figure 2 helps show why this matters. The chart compares stock, bond, and cash returns over rolling 1-, 5-, 10-, and 20-year periods. In all cases, stocks have outperformed on an average annual basis. However, short‑term stock results have varied widely—with one‑year returns ranging from a low of ‑43% to a high of 61%. While the variability of these average stock returns narrows over longer holding periods, they still tend to be higher than bonds and cash. Bottom line: For long‑term investors, there is value in remaining invested and avoiding emotional reactions to short‑term market moves. Importantly, having bonds and cash in your investment mix can help smooth out overall portfolio volatility over time. Asset class returns by holding period (Fig. 2) Past performance cannot guarantee future results. Stocks are represented by the S&P 500 Index. Bonds are represented by the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index. Cash is represented by the 3‑month Treasury bill. Source for Bloomberg index data: Bloomberg Index Services Ltd. Copyright © 2025, Bloomberg Index Services Ltd. Used with permission. Analysis by T. Rowe Price. It is not possible to invest directly in an index. Charts are shown for illustrative purposes. See Additional Disclosures. close Why diversification matters within stocks and bonds Allocating assets between investments like stocks, bonds, and cash is only part of the picture. A well‑built portfolio is also diversified within each asset class, for example, by investment size, style, type, and geographic region. Within stocks, for instance, diversification can include exposure to U.S. large‑, mid‑, and small‑cap stocks, international stocks, and emerging markets stocks. Within bonds, it can include U.S. investment‑grade bonds, Treasuries, international bonds, high yield bonds, and other bond sectors. Diversification matters because leadership within asset classes tends to be cyclical. A part of the market that performs well one year may lag the next. Figure 3 illustrates this clearly by showing how the returns among different stock and bond sectors ranked from 2015 through 2025. This quilt chart supports a simple but important point: Spreading investments across multiple areas of the market can help reduce reliance on any one segment. It also helps expose your portfolio to future top‑performing areas. While diversification cannot assure a profit or protect against loss in a declining market, it remains an important way to manage risk and improve portfolio resilience. Investors can benefit from diversification (Fig. 3) close The following ranges can serve as a starting point when thinking about diversification within a broader portfolio: Within stocks: 60% U.S. large‑cap 25% developed international 10% U.S. small‑cap 5% emerging markets Within bonds: 45% U.S. investment grade 10% to 30% U.S. Treasury 10% nontraditional bond 0% to 10% high yield 10% international 0% to 10% emerging markets It’s important to note that these ranges are examples and are not personalized recommendations. The right mix depends on your broader financial picture, your individual goals, and your comfort level when it comes to investment risk. Asset allocation and saving rate both matter Investment mix is important, but it is only one part of retirement readiness. How much you save also has a major effect on long‑term outcomes. Many investors should aim to save at least 15% of income for retirement, including employer contributions when available through a workplace plan such as a 401(k). If that level is not realistic today, starting lower and increasing the amount over time can still improve long‑term results. A thoughtful retirement plan combines both elements: an investment mix aligned with your goals and a savings rate that supports those goals over time. When to revisit your allocation Your allocation should not stay on autopilot forever. It makes sense to revisit your portfolio in certain situations: you are getting closer to retirement your financial goals change your income or expenses shift meaningfully your tolerance for market volatility changes Reviewing your allocation periodically can help keep your portfolio aligned with your time horizon and retirement needs. A practical takeaway for individual investors A strong retirement portfolio is not built around chasing the best‑performing asset class in any given year. It is built around a mix of investments that fits your goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance. For many individual investors, that means combining stocks, bonds, and cash thoughtfully, diversifying within those categories, saving consistently, and staying focused on long‑term objectives. But do you know if your investments are properly allocated to achieve your goals? Find out with our Portfolio Optimizer .

title: Video Call Hubs for Bangkok Hybrid Teams
summary: When Every Bangkok Workday Includes a Video Call A packed BTS platform, a sudden client escalation, and a calendar full of back-to-back video meetings can turn a productive Bangkok workday into a logistical puzzle. For hybrid teams, freelancers, and business travelers, the challenge is no longer whether people can work remotely; it is whether they […] The post Video Call Hubs for Bangkok Hybrid Teams appeared first on Deskimo .
body_text: When Every Bangkok Workday Includes a Video Call A packed BTS platform, a sudden client escalation, and a calendar full of back-to-back video meetings can turn a productive Bangkok workday into a logistical puzzle. For hybrid teams, freelancers, and business travelers, the challenge is no longer whether people can work remotely; it is whether they can join important calls with the privacy, audio quality, and reliability that professional work demands. This is where call hubs become especially useful. In a city where teams often move between homes, offices, coworking spaces, client sites, cafés, and transit corridors, having access to quiet, bookable spaces for video calls helps people stay responsive without sacrificing professionalism. For Thailand-based teams navigating flexible work, the right setup can reduce stress, protect confidential conversations, and make hybrid collaboration feel far more intentional. Why Call Hubs Matter for Bangkok Hybrid Teams Bangkok has become a practical base for regional teams, digital businesses, entrepreneurs, and global professionals working across time zones. The city offers strong connectivity, a deep service economy, and an increasingly flexible workplace culture. At the same time, hybrid work has exposed a very specific gap: people need more than a laptop and Wi-Fi to communicate well. Call hubs solve a common problem for distributed teams: where do you take a high-stakes video call when your home is noisy, your office is fully booked, or your next appointment is across town? Instead of relying on luck, teams can plan access to professional spaces that support focused communication. The Bangkok-specific friction points Hybrid work in Bangkok is shaped by the city itself. Traffic patterns, weather, dense commercial districts, and long commutes can affect when and where people work. A professional may start the day near Asok, meet a client in Sathorn, and need to join a regional Zoom call before heading to Ari or Ratchada. Without reliable call spaces, the default options are often poor: a noisy café, a hotel lobby, a car, or an open office corner where confidentiality is impossible. These settings can make even experienced professionals appear distracted or unprepared. Common pain points include: Unpredictable background noise from cafés, malls, and shared spaces. Limited private rooms in small offices or coworking areas. Video fatigue caused by poor acoustics and constant interruptions. Confidentiality risks during HR, finance, legal, or client conversations. Commute-related delays that leave little time to return to a main office. Hybrid work is now an operational design issue For HR leaders and business owners, the rise of flexible work is not only an employee preference issue. It is an infrastructure issue. Teams need clear systems for where focused work, collaboration, and confidential calls happen. Thailand continues to position itself as a destination for digital investment and regional business activity. The Thailand Board of Investment highlights the country’s role in attracting business and technology sectors, while the Digital Economy Promotion Agency supports the development of Thailand’s digital ecosystem. As more companies operate with distributed teams, the quality of everyday communication becomes a competitive advantage. In practice, this means hybrid teams need a network of places where people can step into a professional environment quickly. Call hubs are one way to make that possible without committing every employee to a fixed desk or expensive long-term office footprint. What Makes a Good Video Call Hub? Not every quiet-looking room is suitable for a professional video call. A proper video call environment should support privacy, comfort, stable connectivity, and a polished presence. This matters whether someone is pitching to an investor, interviewing a candidate, presenting to a regional leadership team, or discussing sensitive client information. The best spaces are designed around the reality that video calls are not passive tasks. They require concentration, reliable audio, confidence, and sometimes long periods of uninterrupted speaking. Core features to look for When evaluating call hubs in Bangkok or elsewhere in Thailand, focus on the practical details that directly affect meeting quality. A beautiful room is not enough if the audio echoes, the Wi-Fi drops, or people can hear every word from outside. Sound control: Look for enclosed rooms, acoustic treatment, or privacy pods that reduce background noise. Reliable internet: Stable Wi-Fi is essential, especially for screen sharing and multi-person video calls. Good lighting: Natural or well-positioned artificial light improves video presence and reduces fatigue. Comfortable seating: Longer calls require ergonomic support, not just a stool in a corner. Power access: Convenient outlets prevent the panic of a low battery before an important meeting. Easy booking: The space should be simple to reserve, extend, or cancel when schedules change. Professional surroundings: A calm, business-friendly environment helps people feel prepared and focused. For teams that use AI transcription tools or automated meeting assistants, room privacy becomes even more important. If meeting notes include client names, pricing discussions, or internal strategy, the physical environment should support data-conscious behavior. Deskimo has explored this further in why AI note-taking works best with private work rooms , which is especially relevant for teams handling sensitive conversations. Privacy is not a luxury feature Many professionals underestimate how often confidential information is discussed during routine calls. A sales update may reveal revenue targets. A recruitment call may include salary expectations. A client meeting may involve contracts, disputes, or future plans. In open environments, these conversations create unnecessary risk. Even if no one is intentionally listening, sensitive information can be overheard. For Bangkok businesses working with regional partners, regulated industries, or international clients, privacy standards can influence trust. “A professional video call space should protect both the person speaking and the information being shared.” This is why call hubs should be treated as part of a company’s hybrid work policy, not merely as a convenience. Just as businesses secure laptops and cloud systems, they should also think about where employees hold important conversations. How to Build a Practical Call Hub Strategy A strong hybrid work strategy does not require every company to build its own network of rooms. In fact, many teams benefit from a flexible model that combines home offices, company workspaces, coworking access, and on-demand private rooms. The goal is to match the workspace to the task. Not every day requires a desk in a corporate office, but certain meetings do require privacy and stability. A practical strategy helps employees know when to use which option. Map meeting types to workspace needs Start by reviewing the types of video calls your team takes in a typical week. Then decide which calls can happen from home, which require an office, and which are best suited to a professional room near the employee’s location. A simple framework can help: Low-sensitivity calls: Internal check-ins, informal updates, and non-confidential team syncs may be fine from home or a quiet open workspace. Client-facing calls: Sales meetings, onboarding sessions, and account reviews benefit from a polished, quiet setting. Confidential calls: HR matters, legal discussions, finance reviews, and executive meetings should happen in private rooms. High-focus calls: Workshops, interviews, training sessions, and board presentations require comfort, strong Wi-Fi, and minimal interruption. This approach prevents over-engineering. Employees do not need a private room for every conversation, but they should have access to one when the meeting requires it. Create location logic around Bangkok movement patterns Bangkok teams should design around mobility. A workspace plan that assumes everyone can return to one office between meetings may not reflect the reality of the city. Traffic, rain, school schedules, and cross-town appointments can quickly disrupt the day. Instead, think in terms of zones. Employees may need access to workspaces near major business districts, residential clusters, transit stops, and client locations. This is where distributed call hubs can reduce downtime. For example: A sales manager can take a regional partner call near Sukhumvit before visiting a client in Phrom Phong. A recruiter can book a private room near Silom for candidate interviews between office days. A founder can join an investor update near a transit hub instead of rushing back to a fixed office. A consultant can use a professional call room between meetings in Sathorn and Rama IX. Teams in other regional cities face similar challenges when meetings outgrow available office space. The operational thinking behind meeting overflow rooms for Singapore teams applies well to Bangkok too: flexible access can prevent scheduling bottlenecks without expanding permanent real estate. Best Use Cases for Call Hubs in Thailand Different professionals use private video call spaces in different ways. Some need them daily, while others only need them before critical meetings. The value comes from having reliable access at the moment work requires it. In Thailand’s hybrid work environment, call hubs are especially useful for roles that combine mobility, confidentiality, and frequent collaboration. For remote employees and hybrid teams Remote employees often enjoy flexibility, but home is not always the right place for every meeting. Family activity, renovation noise, pets, and shared living arrangements can affect call quality. For employees in condos or shared apartments, private work rooms offer a professional alternative without requiring a full-time office lease. Hybrid teams can use call hubs to support fairness. If some employees have quiet home offices while others do not, meeting performance may be influenced by personal living conditions rather than ability. Providing access to professional call spaces helps level the field. Useful scenarios include: Weekly one-on-ones with managers or direct reports. Regional team meetings across Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, or Australia time zones. Performance reviews and sensitive HR discussions. Online training, webinars, and certification sessions. Interviews and onboarding calls with new hires. For entrepreneurs, consultants, and business travelers Bangkok attracts entrepreneurs, consultants, and visiting executives who often work between appointments. For them, the question is not only where to work, but where to present themselves professionally on short notice. A café may be acceptable for answering emails, but it is rarely ideal for a board update or client negotiation. Hotels can be comfortable, but not always convenient or cost-effective for short calls. A bookable professional room gives business travelers more control over their schedule. Thailand’s economy is closely connected to tourism, services, manufacturing, and regional trade. The Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council provides economic data and national development context that underline Thailand’s role as a major business hub in Southeast Asia. As cross-border business activity grows, mobile professionals need work infrastructure that moves with them. There is also a lesson from transport-connected workspaces. When professionals can work near where they already are, they reduce the hidden cost of travel between meetings. Deskimo’s article on how transit hubs reduce workday friction explains why proximity can be just as important as amenities for modern workdays. How HR and Operations Teams Can Roll This Out For companies, giving employees access to call hubs should be simple, measurable, and aligned with business priorities. The aim is not to encourage unnecessary workspace spending. It is to make sure employees use the right environment for the right work. A clear policy helps employees make good decisions without asking for approval every time they need a quiet place. Set simple usage guidelines Start with practical rules that employees can understand quickly. Avoid making the process too bureaucratic, or people will return to poor workarounds like taking calls in hallways, cars, or noisy cafés. Guidelines might include: Use a private room for client calls where pricing, contracts, or strategy will be discussed. Book a quiet workspace for interviews, performance reviews, or sensitive HR conversations. Use professional call rooms for presentations longer than 30 minutes. Choose locations that reduce travel time between meetings rather than defaulting to the main office. Cancel unused bookings promptly so others can access the space. It can also help to define what employees should not use call rooms for. For example, deep individual work may be better suited to a regular desk unless privacy is required. This keeps availability high for people who genuinely need enclosed meeting space. Track outcomes, not just bookings The value of flexible workspace access should be measured by productivity and experience, not only room usage. HR and operations teams can review how call spaces influence employee stress, meeting quality, and travel efficiency. Consider tracking: Employee satisfaction with hybrid work arrangements. Frequency of missed or delayed calls due to commuting. Feedback from client-facing teams on meeting professionalism. Office room booking pressure during peak meeting hours. Reduction in unnecessary trips back to headquarters. Security-conscious companies can also learn from approaches used in other markets. For example, secure call pods for Australian hybrid teams highlights how privacy-focused spaces support distributed work without weakening professional standards. For Bangkok teams, the key is to make flexible access feel like a normal part of the work toolkit. Employees should know that when a meeting matters, they have a reliable option. Choosing Locations That Actually Improve the Workday The best workspace is not always the one with the most impressive design. It is the one that fits naturally into the employee’s day. In Bangkok, location strategy should account for transit, meeting routes, neighborhood density, and time-of-day movement. Call hubs are most valuable when they remove friction. If a person must travel 40 minutes to reach a room for a 30-minute call, the benefit disappears. A distributed approach works better. Prioritize proximity to work patterns Look at where your team actually spends time. This may include office neighborhoods, client districts, residential areas, and transit-connected zones. A workspace near BTS, MRT, or major road corridors can be more useful than a larger facility in an inconvenient location. For Bangkok-based professionals, practical location priorities often include: Access near central business districts such as Sathorn, Silom, Asok, and Phrom Phong. Options close to transit for employees moving between meetings. Availability near residential zones where remote employees live. Coverage near hotels and conference venues for visiting executives. Easy access to food, transport, and support services between calls. Small time savings compound quickly. If a team of 20 people each saves even one hour per week by using better-located workspaces, the monthly productivity gain is substantial. More importantly, employees feel less rushed and more prepared. Build a better meeting culture around space Workspace access alone will not fix poor meeting habits. Teams should also improve how they schedule and run video calls. A well-designed meeting culture reduces unnecessary calls and makes important ones more effective. Encourage teams to: Share agendas before meetings so participants can prepare. Use asynchronous updates when a live call is not necessary. Protect buffer time between meetings, especially for employees traveling across Bangkok. Choose private rooms for sensitive conversations rather than improvising. Respect end times so others can use booked spaces. The combination of better meeting discipline and better spaces creates a noticeable improvement. People arrive calmer, speak more clearly, and leave with fewer misunderstandings. Make Hybrid Work Feel More Professional and Less Complicated Bangkok’s hybrid teams need flexibility, but they also need reliability. The most effective work setup is not purely remote, purely office-based, or dependent on chance. It gives people access to the right environment at the right time. Call hubs help teams protect confidential conversations, improve video meeting quality, and reduce unnecessary travel across the city. They are useful for remote employees without ideal home offices, entrepreneurs moving between appointments, HR teams handling sensitive discussions, and business travelers who need professional space on demand. For companies in Thailand, the takeaway is straightforward: treat video call environments as part of your hybrid work infrastructure. Map meeting types to space needs, create simple usage guidelines, choose locations around real movement patterns, and measure the impact on productivity and employee experience. With the right approach, call hubs can turn a fragmented workday into a smoother, more professional experience for everyone involved. To book a workspace or download the free Deskimo app . title: I’m 67 With $48,000 in Income. Here’s Exactly How the New $6,000 Senior Deduction Cuts My 2026 Tax Bill.
summary: Retirees may be able to claim an additional $6,000 federal deduction on top of the standard deduction, depending on income and filing status.
body_text: If you’re retired, every tax deduction can make a difference, especially when you’re living on a fixed income. Americans age 65 and older may be able to claim a federal deduction of up to $6,000, but the amount depends on your income and filing status. Here’s how much a 67-year-old with $48,000 in annual income could save on a 2026 federal tax bill. How the Senior Tax Deduction Works If you’re age 65 or older, you may qualify for an additional senior tax break on top of the standard deduction. The maximum benefit is $6,000 per eligible individual for tax years 2025 through 2028. 1 This provision is separate from the existing additional standard deduction available to older taxpayers. If you’re eligible, you may be able to lower more of your taxable income, even if you don’t itemize. To claim the full amount, you generally must meet the following requirements: Rule Explanation Be age 65 or older by the last day of the tax year To claim the additional tax break on your 2026 return, you must have turned 65 by Dec. 31, 2026. Meet the income limits The amount begins to phase out when your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds $75,000 if you’re single or $150,000 if you’re married filing jointly. It gradually decreases as income rises until it phases out completely. Have a valid Social Security number Each person claiming the additional amount must have a valid Social Security number. File a joint return if you’re married Married taxpayers generally must file jointly to claim it. A financial advisor can help you create a tax plan that includes the senior deduction and other breaks you may qualify for. What You Could Save With the Senior Tax Deduction To show how much you could save with the senior deduction, let’s assume you’re a 67-year-old single filer earning $48,000 a year. That income comes from Social Security, a pension and retirement account withdrawals. Your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is below the $75,000 phaseout threshold for single filers (for married couples filing jointly, the threshold is $150,000). To keep the math simple, we’ll treat the full $48,000 as taxable income, even though the taxable portion of Social Security benefits varies from person to person. Without the additional senior deduction, you’d generally claim the 2026 standard deduction ($16,100) and the existing additional standard deduction for single taxpayers age 65 and older ($2,050). 2 That reduces taxable income to $29,850 and results in an estimated federal tax bill of $3,334. Category Amount Total income $48,000 Standard deduction $16,100 Additional standard deduction (age 65+) $2,050 Taxable income before the additional senior deduction $29,850 Estimated federal income tax $3,334 Adding the $6,000 senior deduction lowers taxable income to $23,850, thereby reducing the estimated federal tax bill to $2,614. Category Amount Taxable income before the additional senior deduction $29,850 Additional senior deduction $6,000 Taxable income after the additional senior deduction $23,850 Estimated federal income tax $2,614 In this example, the senior deduction reduces the federal tax bill by about $720. Actual savings will vary because the taxable portion of Social Security benefits differs from one taxpayer to another, and pension income and retirement account withdrawals are not always taxed the same way. Even so, many retirees with similar income could keep several hundred dollars more each year. Additional Retirement Income Can Reduce Your Deduction A larger required minimum distribution (RMD) , higher investment income or additional retirement account withdrawals can push your MAGI past the phase-out threshold, limiting the size of your senior deduction or eliminating it altogether. Timing taxable withdrawals may help preserve more of the available amount. A financial advisor can help manage RMDs and retirement account withdrawals as part of a broader tax strategy. title: How UVA Law Is Maintaining Visibility In A Direct Application World
summary: We recently sat down with Emma Glancy, Senior Assistant Director of the Office of Private Practice at UVA Law, to discuss how UVA is navigating today’s evolving recruiting landscape.
body_text: A Conversation with Emma Glancy, Senior Assistant Director, Office of Private Practice, UVA Law Like many law schools, UVA Law has watched law firm recruiting evolve rapidly over the past several years. As direct applications became increasingly common, the school made a strategic decision to move away from a traditional OCI structure and embrace a more flexible recruiting model. While the transition created new opportunities for students and employers, it also introduced a new challenge: re-creating visibility. Without bidding systems and centralized interview schedules, counselors emphasized individualized communication with students to continue to understand where students were applying, how engaged they were, and where they might need support. We recently sat down with Emma Glancy, Senior Assistant Director of the Office of Private Practice at UVA Law, to discuss how UVA is navigating today’s evolving recruiting landscape and why greater visibility has become increasingly important as recruiting continues to shift toward direct applications . Q: UVA made the decision to move away from OCI. What drove that change? Emma : We were seeing more and more students apply directly to firms rather than through traditional recruiting programs, with many firms expressing their preference for this model. Flo shared data with us showing how much recruiting activity was already happening through direct applications, and it reinforced what we were seeing ourselves. Flo: As more schools experience similar shifts, many are evaluating how to support students in an increasingly direct application environment while reducing administrative complexity. For UVA, embracing that trend also created an opportunity to rethink how student recruiting activity could be monitored outside of a traditional OCI structure. Q: What was the biggest challenge after stepping away from OCI? Emma: We did lose some of the visibility that we would have otherwise had through hosting an OCI program. With OCI, you naturally have access to bidding information and interview schedules. You know who’s participating and where students are engaging. Once recruiting becomes more decentralized, you lose some of that built-in insight. We’re grateful that our students do such a wonderful job working closely with us every step of the process, but having a way to better understand where students are in the process at a glance would be incredibly beneficial for counselors and students alike. That’s where Flo Forward will help bridge the gap in visibility. Q: How has Flo Forward helped recreate that visibility? Emma: The application tracking and reporting tools are incredibly helpful. Being able to quickly see where students are applying, how many applications they have submitted, and whether interviews are progressing will help us have more efficient, productive counseling sessions focused on strategy and guidance. That visibility will help us identify where students may need support while also giving students time back that they may have been spending tracking their applications. Just having that snapshot is a win-win for all of us. Flo : As more students use Flo Forward to organize their job searches, that visibility continues to become even more valuable. Students can now track opportunities beyond those posted directly on Flo Forward, which will help schools better understand the full scope of their recruiting activity and have more informed advising conversations. We’re also excited to include Public Interest opportunities to the platform. Many students pursue a variety of career paths, and having more of those opportunities represented in one place will make it easier for students to stay organized while giving your office a more complete picture of how they’re navigating the recruiting process. This combination of student-driven tracking and advisor visibility helps create a more connected recruiting experience for both students and career services. Q: How has the Recruiting Tracker impacted your office? Emma: For several years, our team has spent countless hours creating our own internal resource that mirrors Flo’s recruiting tracker. Now, Flo’s recruiting tracker has taken the laboring oar of updating available opportunities, mitigating our need to maintain spreadsheets and search each firm’s website for current information. Q: How will you use the Event Board as part of your recruiting strategy? Emma : Recently, we updated our recruiting guidelines to allow firms more flexibility in hosting off-Grounds events with our students. We love working with law firms to help them plan out and schedule their events with our students, but are more limited in our ability to market each firm’s individual events, and don’t provide employers with class-wide student contact lists. The Event Dashboard helps firms promote opportunities directly to UVA Law students, while also providing us with visibility into student participation. Flo: Beyond employer-hosted events, schools can also add their own programming, creating a more centralized destination for students to discover recruiting opportunities. As students register through the Event Board, participation is shared back with the career services office, providing additional insight into student engagement and helping schools better understand which programming resonates most with their students. It’s beneficial for employers, students, and schools. Q: Recruiting timelines continue to move earlier. How does Flo Forward help students navigate that environment? Emma : Law schools operate on different timelines, and we constantly tell our students, “It’s a marathon, not a sprint.” If our students hear that their peers at other law schools are progressing in the recruiting cycle, being aware of those schools’ exam periods and grade release dates helps to contextualize their timing and encourage them to focus on running their own race. By bringing that information together in one place, the reporting ecosystem makes that context readily accessible. Q: What role does Flo Forward play in the overall student experience? Emma: One of the biggest benefits is centralization. Students are juggling applications, interviews, networking events, callbacks, and research across multiple employers and timelines. Flo Forward brings much of that activity into one place. Students can research employers, track applications, manage interviews, register for events, and stay organized throughout the process. Having a one-stop shop for students to send out their applications rather than navigating to every single law firm portal saves valuable time, and time is a limited resource in this accelerated cycle. Anything we can do to simplify the recruiting experience for students is a win. Q: As you look ahead, what are you most excited about? Emma : Overall, we’re just really excited to have a cohesive space for our 1Ls to conduct their job search, submit applications, and participate in interviews, that also gives us as CSOs real-time visibility into where they’re at in the process. Conclusion As law schools like UVA navigate the changing recruiting landscape, Flo Forward offers new ways to improve visibility into student recruiting activity while reducing administrative effort. Features like application tracking, the Recruiting Tracker, the Event Board, and enhanced reporting are designed to help career services teams spend less time managing processes and more time supporting students. To learn more about becoming a Flo Forward Partner School, contact the Flo team.
